articles.title: Why US soldiers keep killing women in Okinawa — and why they go unpunished
articles.author: Amanda Yee
articles.content: In October, 39-year-old Ann Yagi was found dead in a Naha hotel. Shortly after, US marine Devin Jacob Ballard was arrested on charges of murder-robbery. But the Yagi’s killing reignited a decades-old question Okinawa can’t escape: Who pays the price for Washington’s military bases? Okinawan scholar and peace activist Keiko Yonaha joins Amanda Yee to lay out what the headlines leave out — countless sexual assaults by US soldiers and near-total impunity, a Japanese government that covers up case after case, and what Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s rapid militarization means for an island already marked as a potential battlefield. Yonaha also takes direct aim at the new Cold War narrative driving it all, arguing there is no “China threat” to Okinawa or Japan, that the story is being amplified by right-wing trolls and pro-government media to manufacture consent for war. The real danger, she warns, is the US strategy seeking to turn Japan and Okinawa into a frontline for war with China.

articles.title: Algeria sends troops to Niger as security ties deepen
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: On October 30, the first convoy of Algerian troops arrived in its southern neighbor Niger as security ties continue to deepen between the two countries. It is Algeria’s first foreign deployment since it sent troops to Egypt during the 1973 Arab-Israeli war. The deployment was approved by both houses of the parliament on October 25. “Niger’s security is part of Algeria’s security,” said Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf, who tabled the proposal before legislators. Algeria shares a 951 km-long border with Niger in the Sahara Desert, which became a hotbed for terror groups after the destruction of Libya by NATO powers in 2011. Groups affiliated with Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State have carried out multiple attacks in recent times in Niger, where Algeria has strategic energy projects. Strategic infrastructure In August, Algeria and Niger jointly laid the foundation stone for a project to explore four wells in the Kafra oil field in Niger’s northern Agadez region, about 85 km south of the Algerian border. ​ The Algerian state oil company Sonatrach, whose subsidiary ENAFOR is drilling, holds a 50% stake in the project. Its Nigerien counterpart, Sonidep, holds the other half. Niger’s petroleum ministry estimates the potential at 2.5 billion barrels.​ A subsidiary of Algeria’s state-owned electricity and gas utility group Sonelgaz built the 40-Megawatt Algerian–Nigerien Solidarity Power Plant in Niger’s capital, Niamey, earlier in June.​ That month Algeria also started constructing its section of the Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline (TSGP) to transport 30 billion cubic meters of natural gas from Nigeria to Algeria’s Hassi R’Mel hub, from where it is to be exported to Europe through the Trans-Mediterranean Pipeline.​ At a total length of 4,128 km, the TSGP is to span three countries. 2,310 km of this pipeline will be laid in Algeria, which owns a 45% stake in the project through Sonatrach. 1,039 km will be in the origin country, Nigeria, whose state-owned petroleum company owns another 45%. The 841 km in the middle will run through Niger, which owns the remaining 10% through Sonidep. It is to protect such critical infrastructure that the Algerian deployment is to be made, at the request of Niger, Attaf told the legislators. “We are not sending our soldiers to wage war in Niger, but for a mission to secure economic infrastructure,” added Senator Belkacem Boulghiti, addressing the media after the parliament voted to approve the deployment. A deepening military cooperation While the deployment itself may have this limited mission of guarding infrastructure, a much deeper military cooperation is developing between the two countries. Earlier, on October 21, Niger’s Minister of National Defense, General Salifou Modi, visited Algeria.​ He met the Algerian army’s chief of staff, General Saïd Chanegriha, who expressed “Algeria’s readiness to consider any proposal from Niger that could strengthen military and security cooperation, serving the best interests of both brotherly countries.”​ In that meeting, they signed a memorandum of understanding for “cooperation and exchange of experiences in the field of the fight against terrorism, as well as responding to any project requested by the Nigerien authorities aimed at strengthening the operational capabilities of the Nigerien army.”​ Four days later, parliament approved troop deployment. The troops will be stationed at Madama, a military base strategically located in Niger’s north, near the Libyan border. “This site occupies a strategic position for monitoring the Sahel region and cross-border routes,” said former Algerian diplomat Amar Belani, recalling that it was “a former French support point developed as part of Operation Barkhane,” which started in 2014. ​However, this French operation, meant to suppress the terror groups it helped spawn across the Sahel by participating in the destruction of Libya in 2011, was a failure as armed violence only rose alongside increasing French troops.​ Barkhane unraveled eight years later amid a wave of anti-France protests leading to popularly-supported coups that ousted the France-backed governments in its former colonies, bringing in military governments that went on to expel the French troops: Mali in 2022, Burkina Faso in early 2023, and Niger later that year.​ Diplomatic rift and revival Algeria joined the chorus condemning the coups in all three countries, which went on to form the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) in late 2023. This had already caused a strain on the diplomatic relations between Algeria and the AES countries, when, in April 2025, Algeria shot down a Malian drone that was targeting terror groups in its border region of Kidal.​ Algeria claimed that the drone had crossed into its airspace. Mali refuted the claim. All three AES members, including Niger, withdrew their ambassadors from Algeria. Algeria reciprocated.​ Over the next months, attacks by Al-Qaeda and IS-affiliated groups intensified in all the AES states, which have long been accusing France of backing these groups to destabilize their countries for asserting sovereignty and breaking free from French neocolonial rule.​ Algeria had not only fought the French for its independence but also the Islamist extremist groups within in a bitter civil war in the 90s. Al-Qaeda and IS growing in Mali and Niger is perceived as a threat to Algeria, which shares a total of over 2,310 km of land border with the two Sahelian neighbors. ​ In February 2026, Algerian president Abdelmadjid Tebboune invited his Nigerien counterpart Abdourahamane Tchiani to Algeria for a meeting, where they agreed to restore diplomatic relations at the highest level.​ Read more: Mali and Algeria revitalize diplomatic relations after falling out last year “In the face of ongoing terrorist threats and the ongoing organized border crime, the leaders of the two countries expressed their concern for each other’s security and said that the security of one is inseparable from the security of the other,” read a statement by the Algerian presidency.​ “With this spirit of effective solidarity, they agreed to immediately activate the Algerian-Nigerian mechanisms concerned to intensify coordination in border surveillance and coordinate strategies for combating terrorism.” They also agreed to develop closer cooperation in the field of agriculture, healthcare, and infrastructure.​ “We will protect Niger no matter what”​ In August, Algeria donated two Mi-24V helicopters, two Mi-171 helicopters, and associated military equipment. Later that month, following a failed mutiny on August 29, Algeria deployed more aircraft, including four Sukhoi Su-30 fighter jets and an aerial refueling aircraft to Air Base 101 in Niger’s capital, Niamey.​ “There are countries, which I will not name, that have conspired against (Niger). We stand by its side,” Tebboune said in a televised address on October 3. Niger itself has named France, France-backed governments in the neighborhood – including Chad, Benin, and Côte d’Ivoire – and Ukraine as assisting terror groups to destabilize the country after it expelled French troops.​ “Today, we have interests. We have reached agreements (with Niger) in the oil, mining and other sectors, and some are seeking to destroy all of this overnight,” added Tebboune, declaring, “We will protect Niger no matter what.”​ Algeria has the second-most powerful military in Africa. While AES countries had developed a security partnership with Russia to help combat terror groups after expelling French troops, the entry of Algeria as a security partner advances the principle of ‘African solutions to African problems’, adopted by the African Union (AU) as an official position in Agenda 2063.​ Meanwhile, Algeria and Mali also mutually reinstated their ambassadors in July. On the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in September, Algeria’s foreign minister Attaf also met his Burkinabe counterpart, Karamoko Traoré. The ministers not only discussed how to revive bilateral relations and strengthen ties but also “the main security and development challenges facing the region.”​

articles.title: Over 4,000 arrested under Palestine Action ban
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: New arrests of Palestine solidarity activists on October 31 brought the total number of arrests related to the Palestine Action ban in Britain to over 4,000, advocacy groups warned on Saturday. The arrests were made during an action in front of the US embassy in London, as law enforcement agencies once again decided to charge protesters holding signs expressing their opposition to the genocide in Gaza. The action was mirrored in the proximity of the US consulate in Edinburgh, where no arrests were made on the day. Since July 2025 – when Keir Starmer’s government proscribed direct action group Palestine Action – police forces around the country have disrupted peaceful protests against the ban. This has led to legal consequences for thousands of people, many of them elderly people, public service workers, and healthcare professionals. A dual action was held in front of US diplomatic offices in London and Edinburgh on Saturday, October 31. Source: Defend Our Juries/Marly Lyman “Including the arrests so far today, there have been over 4,000 arrests of people under section 11, 12 and 13 of the Terrorism Act 2000 for expressing support for Palestine Action, whether for taking part in a vigil, recording an online video message or for encouraging others to support the banned group,” Defend Our Juries stated on Saturday. “These arrests contributed to a 1,186% rise in the total number of terrorism-related arrests in the year ending March 2026, whilst almost half of all terrorism arrests since 9/11 in the United Kingdom have come in the year to September 2026.” Watch: Why the US just branded Palestine Action ‘global terrorists’ Activists have claimed former prime minister Starmer imposed the ban at least in part to appease US President Donald Trump, echoing the latter’s strategy of targeting progressives. “The ban on Palestine Action was straight out of Trump’s playbook, so it’s fitting that this significant milestone has been reached on Halloween and outside the US Embassy, laying bare the terrifying attacks on free speech that this authoritarian ban has unleashed,” Defend Our Juries said. Many also believe that Palestine Action’s proscription in Britain facilitated the terrorist designation imposed on the organization by the Trump administration in August this year. Authors and academics treated as terrorists In Britain, the Palestine Action ban remains contested in court by the group’s co-founder Huda Ammori, and has drawn pronounced criticism for the chilling effect it has had on freedom of expression and the right to protest. Several examples over the past year have shown these are not trivial concerns. The latest is the barring of left author, academic, and outspoken Palestine solidarity proponent Andreas Malm from entering the UK as he was scheduled to participate in a public event together with Ammori. On Friday, Tribune reported that the scholar’s travel authorization had been revoked, with the Home Office saying that his “presence in the UK is not considered to be conducive to the public good.” Read more: Hasan Piker and Cenk Uygur blocked from entering UK “He is being censored for speaking out against censorship, in truly Orwellian fashion,” said Tribune editor Oliver Eagleton . “It is shameful that Andy Burnham’s government is continuing the authoritarian overreach we saw under Keir Starmer, and in this dystopian new reality it is now commonplace in Britain for authors and academics to be treated as terrorists because they support Palestinians facing genocide and the rights of people protesting that genocide.” “This is not an isolated incident – and the government should know that it is gaining a bad reputation for censorship and repression,” Your Party MP Jeremy Corbyn wrote on social media. “We know why the government has taken this decision: because it wants to silence criticism of Israel, as well as its own complicity in genocide. It will not succeed.” “What future governments might do with this power should frighten us all” Earlier in October, Irish novelist Sally Rooney announced her books would no longer be available in Britain as a result of her expressed support for Palestine Action. The announcement triggered mass support for Rooney among authors, poets, and editors, who said it is unconscionable that “a government can now effectively ban a single author for protesting that government’s own conflation of protest with terrorism.” “What future governments might do with this power should frighten us all.” “I can’t say that I am standing up for the children of Wales if I allow the children of Gaza to be murdered and mutilated without comment,” said Nicola Davies, the Children’s Laureate for Wales, announcing her decision to donate royalties from one of her books to Rooney. “Gaza is smaller than the Welsh county of Flintshire and it’s as if all Wales children were concentrated there and being bombed.”

articles.title: “Princes and Thieves” Author Matthew Cole on Jared Kushner & the “Secret Plot to Remake Middle East”
articles.content: Vanity Fair recently published an excerpt from longtime investigative reporter Mathhew Cole’s new book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East . The excerpt alleged that during President Trump’s first term, Saudi and Emirati leaders secretly put at least $2 billion into bank accounts and gave access to Kushner. At the time, Jared Kushner was serving as senior adviser to President Trump, his father-in-law. He is now Trump’s special envoy. Kushner’s lawyers responded by demanding that Vanity Fair retract the article and threatening legal action against the book publisher, Simon & Schuster. Jared Kushner denied the report, saying, “The allegations made by this author are completely insane, categorically false, and never happened. We denied every one of these claims on the record, yet the author failed to provide a single shred of evidence to substantiate any of them.” His lawyers say no such bank accounts existed and that the allegations are unsupported by the verifiable evidence. In an extended interview with Democracy Now! , author Matthew Cole stood by his reporting. “This book is a result of more than 50 sources. There was an enormous amount of fact-checking and legal vetting that went into this book,” says Cole. “There’s plenty of information and reporting in the book that lets us establish and understand that there was … an unholy alliance between Jared Kushner and the leader of the UAE , the leader of Saudi Arabia and, at the time, Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of Israel.” On Friday, Congressmember Jamie Raskin, the ranking Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, called on Kushner to recuse himself from Middle East and Ukraine negotiations and to produce a “comprehensive list of bank accounts or other financial instruments” that he had access to during his time in government.

articles.title: “Ungrounding”: Eyal Weizman on Gaza Genocide & Israel’s “Permanent Architecture of Control”
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : Israel is continuing to commit genocide in Gaza long past the so-called ceasefire agreement. That’s according to a new report out this week from the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. The report also accuses Israeli forces of committing crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, torture and rape. The Israeli Mission in Geneva said the latest report was part of a “misinformation campaign to demonize the State of Israel” and to, quote, “destroy the Jewish state,” unquote. The United Nations-commissioned experts said Israel was, quote, “continuing to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza,” unquote. They found Israeli forces continued using heavy munitions, drones, quadcopters, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas during the ceasefire. They also found that the so-called Yellow Line, which was presented as a temporary ceasefire demarcation, is increasingly encroaching into Gaza and becoming a de facto border. Well, the organization Forensic Architecture, which has been mapping Israel’s military conduct in Gaza since October 2023, details exactly how Israel has used the Yellow Line to expand its territorial control of Gaza. Here’s a clip from the project titled “A Cartography of Genocide.” NARRATOR : When the ceasefire came into effect, most of the area Israel had depopulated remained under its control. This constituted 54% of Gaza, marked by the Yellow Line. The Yellow Line is meant to mark phase one of Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza. Instead, Israel is using the line to expand its control. Along the Yellow Line, Israel has placed concrete yellow blocks, signaling areas Palestinians cannot approach. We have mapped the position of more than 100 yellow blocks. Most have been placed well beyond the agreed withdrawal line. Over time, Israel is moving these blocks further into the area where Palestinians are concentrated. With every expansion, the military destroys another neighborhood, preventing Palestinian return. Israel also imposed an additional boundary, which it called the Orange Line. In some places, this line encroaches more than one kilometer beyond the Yellow Line. At the same time, Israel has entrenched its military presence. Around every 1.8 kilometers along the Yellow Line, it has built a fortified military base. We have documented 34 active bases. Many bases, like this one in Bani Suheila, have been constructed on the ruins of Palestinian homes. Israel has also demolished and compacted nearby buildings which remained standing. Building by building, Gaza’s landscape is being permanently reconfigured. This picture shows the neighborhood before it was erased. AMY GOODMAN : On Tuesday, the U.N. special rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Francesca Albanese, called on the ICC , the International Criminal Court, to investigate incitement to genocide by government officials and media figures in Israel. FRANCESCA ALBANESE : What is happening is not incidental; it is intentional. This is why I provocatively called it mediacide, the systematic destruction of the media’s public function, the transformation of media itself into an instrument through which atrocities can be concealed, normalized or justified. In a genocide, the systematic attack on the media is part and parcel of the crime. AMY GOODMAN : Over 250 Palestinian journalists and media workers have been killed in Gaza since October 2023. To talk about Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and more, we’re joined here in New York by Eyal Weizman, the Israeli-born British architect, the founder and director of Forensic Architecture. His book is just out. It’s called Ungrounding: The Architecture of Genocide . Eyal is professor of spatial and visual cultures at Goldsmiths College at the University of London. His previous books include Hollow Land, Israel’s Architecture of Occupation and The Least of All Possible Evils: A Short History of Humanitarian Violence . Eyal Weizman is a member of the Technology Advisory Board of the International Criminal Court and the recipient of the 2024 Right Livelihood Award, also known as the Alternative Nobel Prize. Eyal Weizman, welcome back to Democracy Now! EYAL WEIZMAN : It’s such a pleasure being here, Amy. AMY GOODMAN : Let’s turn first to the title of your book. It’s called Ungrounding: The Architecture of Genocide . If you can explain what that means? EYAL WEIZMAN : Yeah. So, in Forensic Architecture, we often look at cities that undergo an aerial bombardment campaign. And even after those bombings, you can see where buildings have stood. You can see a pile of ruin. Ungrounding is a kind of destruction that we have not seen anywhere else. It is actually produced by bulldozers, and nothing has remained of the traces of destruction. In fact, the bulldozer stab their front loader into the ground and flips the terrain, erasing also the traces of destruction. So, ungrounding is a kind of destruction that traces — that erases the traces of destruction. It’s producing a kind of desertification, if you like, a kind of homogeneous piles of ruin that are unidentified by the people that inhabited that place before. AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to turn to a part of that short video that your group, Forensic Architecture, made about the living conditions in Gaza since the start of the so-called ceasefire. NARRATOR : Inside the concentration area, the majority of Palestinians still live in sprawling tent camps. The population density and Israel’s ongoing siege are severely limiting access to resources. This orchard in Khan Younis was one of the few still accessible to Palestinians. Since the ceasefire, it has been cleared to make room for tents. Degraded living conditions are becoming the permanent reality of life in Gaza. Tent camps are surrounded by destruction, and many Palestinians have resorted to sheltering inside and around damaged buildings. On the 16th of September, one of these buildings collapsed, killing at least 20 Palestinians. Three years into the genocide, the ceasefire is normalizing ongoing Israeli occupation and expansion, while Palestinian life is slowly being extinguished. AMY GOODMAN : That’s an excerpt of a clip from Forensic Architecture. And since we’re spending the hour, Eyal Weizman, I’m wondering if you can explain what this group does. Because when talking about issues like genocide, why would we be talking about architecture? Talk about the importance of place and erasure and changing the actual geography of where people live. EYAL WEIZMAN : So, one of the prohibitions of the Genocide Convention speaks about the destructions of a people’s conditions of life. A people’s life, human life, depends on the environment that sustain it. It depends on buildings, on home, depends on infrastructure. It depends on hospitals. It depends on agriculture and open areas. In the Genocide Convention, or in Raphael Lemkin, who actually framed the concept of genocide and understood that you can kill a people indirectly by destroying whatever it is that is necessary to sustain life. The result of that, unlike the fast or hot components of genocide, where people are executed, murdered, thrown into mass graves, etc., is a genocide by attrition, is a much longer and much more extended process of genocide. And in fact, genocide by the destruction of conditions of life is typical of settler-colonial genocide. Think about the genocides undertaken in the Americas. It has taken decades or centuries to destroy entire cultures by displacing people, by destroying the environment that they depend on for culture, for sustenance. And that is what we’re seeing happening in Gaza. It is one of the speeds of the genocides that is happening in Gaza. And I think that since the ceasefire, the so-called ceasefire, began in October 2025, the destruction of the Palestinian people by the destruction and degrading of their environment is the most pronounced means of destroying Palestinian life in the southwestern coast of Palestine, that is also known as the Gaza Strip. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Eyal Weizman, you talk not only about the United States’s weapons to Israel that are used, but also the companies that participate in this ungrounding — for instance, the giant Caterpillar tractors that move much of the rubble and destroy buildings. But you also note in your book, and I quote you, “The Caterpillars have been here for a long time. In August 1950 the area that came to be known as the Gaza Strip was cut off from the rest of Palestine by a ditch carved into the soil by a single-blade plough pulled by a tractor. An archival photograph depicting the scene shows the tractor to be a Second World War-era Caterpillar, model.” And could you talk about that and these American companies that also assist the Israelis in this ungrounding? EYAL WEIZMAN : Yeah, I was very surprised during my research to find that the Gaza Strip was created, in fact, with a plow, with a plow line, just like, you know, Rome, the legend of Rome, carved — whose border was carved by a plow. The Caterpillars are an earth-transforming instrument and incredibly useful in Israeli settler-colonial destruction, which is about transforming the environment. There’s a lot of speak now about Israeli use of AI in targeted bombing and mass surveillance, etc. At the end, what we’re seeing on the ground is much simpler. It’s a kind of the result of — that could have been in any historical settler-colonial genocide: total erasure, ungrounding, the transformation of the environment undertaken by those big monster of technical equipment, manufactured by Caterpillar here, which produce, in fact, the architecture of genocide. Right now since the so-called ceasefire began, it has become possible, or more possible, for private companies that use American and European-made bulldozers and excavators to actually enter into the Gaza Strip. Previously, during — before the ceasefire, it was — they had to be insured with a lot of money. Now the ground transformation, what we call terraforming, of Gaza has been accelerated. And there is — just Gaza has turned into an enormous construction site by Israeli-operated, U.S.-made excavators of that, such that are transforming the landscape, that are building roads and military bases, that none of that manifestation of the environmental transformation of Gaza points to the fact that Israel is intending to follow the next clauses or obligation that it has under the ceasefire agreement — i.e., withdrawal from Gaza. They are setting a permanent architecture of control made out of all the rubble and ruins of Palestinian homes. The rubble and ruin of Palestinian home are piled into that landscape, that there is a giant earth berm, six meter high, now being stretched all along the — what is called the Orange Line, which is one kilometer further into Gaza than the Yellow Line. It is leaving only some 30-something percent of the Gaza Strip for the survivors of the genocide in Gaza, all along a 40-kilometer-long earth berm, six meters high, made of thousands and thousands of Palestinian homes. Now, many of those homes were actually bombed during and before the so-called ceasefire. There are bodies. In fact, we are mapping the location of bodies of Palestinians that could not be extracted under the rubble of their own home. We know there are about 10,000 Palestinians missing. Many of them are under the rubble. And when Israel is shuffling that rubble into all sort of shapes and berms and military bases and roads, they are actually moving human remains. So, in addition to Francesca Albanese’s, you know, the report on the killing of Palestinian, murder of Palestinian journalists, we know that the shuffling of that rubble is destroying evidence for the genocide. Israel is actively and against court order, against the order of the ICJ , destroying the evidence of the genocide that it has perpetrated. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Eyal Weizman, in your book, you talk not only about the destruction of the soil, but of the — you talk also about the subsoil and the hundreds of miles of underground tunnels that remain the only, as you say, unoccupied part of Palestine. Could you talk about that and how the Israelis have attempted to deal with that? EYAL WEIZMAN : Yeah. So, the book — the book really is a hundred-year history of the southwestern coast of Palestine. It’s divided into a chapter dealing with soil, with the agriculture of the Indigenous population, and then the agricultural settler colonialism built in its stead by Zionist colonies around Gaza. And it describes the emergence of the tunnel project, indeed made by Indigenous Palestinians, many of which are farmers who knew how to dig wells in that threshold, in a part of Palestine that is close to the desert, where digging for water is so important and so complicated. Some of the traditional wells of the Palestinians, 200,000 Palestinians that were displaced into the Gaza Strip during 1948, were incredible Indigenous knowledge in knowing how to dig tunnels. They were made landless in the Gaza Strip, thrown onto the sand dunes along the coast, but knew how to build a project, a subterranean project, that was made initially to bypass the siege that was imposed on Gaza. Gaza has always had a very robust trade with Egypt. I mean, in fact, the oldest trade route in the world, that the Romans called the Via Maris, runs from Alexandria through Gaza to the rest of Palestine and then the Levant. That trade route was cut by the formation of the Gaza Strip, and then the border between Palestine and Egypt. And the trade was running through the subsoil. So, the tunnel project began as a means to alleviate the conditions of life that Israel imposed on Gaza. Only later, it became a military, a resistance project — in fact, I would say, one of the greatest pieces of architecture of liberation, if you like. Palestinians may have lost control of the land, but controlled entirely the subsoil. So, while about 85% of all buildings that were standing in Gaza prior to October 7th, 2023, are destroyed, only the opposite number of tunnels have been destroyed. The majority of the tunnel project is still intact. It could withstand Israeli bombardment. But tunnels are also Israel’s excuse for ungrounding. So, be they as effective as they are, they are located in specific places, but Israel destroys continuously the totality of the surface and the subsoil in places that it occupies, and based that destruction on the existence of tunnels. Israel likes to call the tunnel project “the metro,” as if every point is connected to everything else, creating an image of totality in the subsoil. But indeed, if it would have been a metro, that would have been the dumbest thing to do, because, you know, you expose one connection, and you can travel all along and expose the entire tunnel project. It’s nothing like that, but Israel liked to create that impression in order to justify its total destruction of every area, every neighborhood, of every building, every home, every school, every university, every public building, orchard, field, in areas that it occupies. AMY GOODMAN : Last year, during a joint news conference at the White House with the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump, CNN’s Kaitlan Collins questioned Trump about his plan for Gaza. KAITLAN COLLINS : Just to follow up on what you were saying about the Gazans leaving Gaza, going to other countries, one, where exactly are you suggesting that they should go? And, two, are you saying they should return after it’s rebuilt? And if not, who do you envision living there? PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : I envision world people living there, the world’s people. I think you’ll make that into an international, unbelievable place. I think the potential in the Gaza Strip is unbelievable. And I think the entire world, representatives from all over the world, will be there, and they’ll — KAITLAN COLLINS : But not the Palestinians? PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : — and they’ll live there. Palestinians also. Palestinians will live there. Many people will live there. But they’ve tried the other, and they’ve tried it for decades and decades and decades. It’s not going to work. It didn’t work. It will never work. And you have to learn from history. History has — you know, you just can’t let it keep repeating itself. We have an opportunity to do something that could be phenomenal. And I don’t want to be cute. I don’t want to be a wise guy. But the riviera of the Middle East, this could be something that could be so — this could be so magnificent. AMY GOODMAN : That riviera “could be so magnificent.” And back in 2024, Trump’s son-in-law, former adviser Jared Kushner weighed in on Israel’s war on Gaza, saying Israel should move Palestinians out of the besieged territory, which he said contains “very valuable waterfront property,” made the remarks during an event hosted by the Middle East Initiative at the Harvard Kennedy School. JARED KUSHNER : And Gaza’s waterfront property, it could be very valuable to — if people would focus on kind of building up, you know, livelihoods. You think about all the money that’s gone into this tunnel network and into all the munitions, if that would have gone into education or innovation, what could have been done. And so, I think that it’s a little bit of an unfortunate situation there, but I think, from Israel’s perspective, I would do my best to move the people out and then clean it up. But I don’t think that Israel has stated that they don’t want the people to move back there afterwards. AMY GOODMAN : If you can respond, Eyal Weizman, author of Ungrounding: The Architecture of Genocide ? EYAL WEIZMAN : This is clearly — that architectural plan, development plan, is the continuation of genocide by other means. As we heard, the plan is to remove everybody from the construction site by all sort of excuses — the area is too dangerous, they need a place for the reconstruction, need to fence up the building site, etc. When Palestinians were pushed out of Palestine, they were never historically allowed to return. And there is no reason to believe that if that ludicrous plan is ever coming into fruition — and I don’t see any indication that it does; all I see is further misery and the kind of strangulation of the population inside this concentration area in Gaza. But if it does, this is — Palestinians will not be allowed to return. In the crime of genocide, it could be actually undertaken by destruction, as we have seen, and genocide could be undertaken by reconstruction as a means of destroying a particular national life in that part. And the only people that are not asked what to reconstruct, how they want to live in that area of the Gaza Strip, are Palestinian architects. But what I see is Palestinian families wanting to return and establish the location of where the house once stood, now mostly dunes of earth and rubble, and rebuild there, next to their community, alongside their neighbors, etc., making the reconstruction actually part of a community rebuilding of the survivors. And I want to remind us that the return of Palestinians to their homes inside the Gaza Strip and building it on their own terms is absolutely essential, but it’s not the full picture. Palestinians are refugees. Their homes are in areas that is now Israel, and their right of return is actually recognized by the U.N. So, whatever reconstruction would occur temporarily in Gaza is not the full undoing of the crime against the Palestinian people. AMY GOODMAN : Eyal Weizman, we’re going to break, then come back to this discussion, founder and director of Forensic Architecture, latest book, Ungrounding: The Architecture of Genocide . Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : “Really Real,” Allison Russell and Ganessa James of Rainbow Coalition, performing in our Democracy Now! studio. This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González, as we continue our conversation with Eyal Weizman, founder and director of Forensic Architecture, out with a new book, Ungrounding: The Architecture of Genocide . Now, Congressmember Rashida Tlaib recently called on the Department of Justice to arrest the Israeli military commander Sean Glass, accused of killing 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab. In 2024, she and six of her relatives were killed as they hid inside the family’s car while attempting to evacuate Gaza City. That was in 2024. Two paramedics from the Palestine Red Crescent who attempted to rescue them after Hind called them for help were also killed. Eyal, your organization, Forensic Architecture, investigated the killings. The findings were featured in the Al Jazeera Fault Lines documentary The Night Won’t End: Biden’s War on Gaza . This clip features Nicholas Masterton of Forensic Architecture, beginning with Fault Lines correspondent Sharif Abdel Kouddous. SHARIF ABDEL KOUDDOUS : Based off that range from the sound analysis, combined with satellite imagery and photos of the area around the current gas station, they were also able to examine where the shooting could have come from. LAYAN HAMADEH : [translated] They’re shooting at us. The tank is next to me. NICHOLAS MASTERTON : We marked all of the bullet holes that we could see from those images. There are holes which appear to be exit holes, so larger openings that are flared, that we witness more on one side of the car than the other. So this gives us a kind of general direction as to the direction of fire. So, there’s one very distinct line of bullets that we can see at the back, the rear right-hand side of the car, which is a volley of about 30 or so bullets. You’ll remember at the end of Fabio’s analysis, we saw this ring. And what we were able to do is to superimpose this ring onto the site of the killing. So, we situate the 3D model of the car inside of the site, and we position it in its resting position outside the gas station. And we’re also able to model the Merkava tank, and we’re able to direct the weapons on the tank towards the car. And this is important, because it allows us to draw a line between the guns on the tank and the entry holes that we see on the Kia. So, based on positioning the tank in hundreds of places within that ring of 13 to 23 meters, we find that there’s a position immediately to the south of the Kia, which appears to be the most likely position of the shooter, for this recording. SHARIF ABDEL KOUDDOUS : So, from what you’ve assessed of the Israeli tank position at that distance, is it likely the Israeli soldiers would have been able to see who was in the car? NICHOLAS MASTERTON : We think that it’s very likely that they would have been able to see who was in the car, because we know that these tanks are fitted with optical equipment, which allows them to see for many kilometers. So, yeah, it seems very likely that whatever was going on in the car 13 meters away would have been easily visible. AMY GOODMAN : So, that’s a clip of what Forensic Architecture has done in explaining, in investigating what happened to Hind Rajab and her family. And again, Rashida Tlaib, the U.S. congressmember, is calling on the military commander in charge of the company responsible for the family’s and the paramedics’ deaths — calling for the arrest of Sean Glass, who commanded the “Vampire Empire” Company. He is a former Navy SEAL who joined the IDF . Now, Eyal Weizman, I wanted to ask you — put this in a larger context. And that larger context is the — Forensic Architecture is working with the ICC to produce evidence for the genocide case against Israel. Can you talk about the techniques you’re using, the evidence that’s required to prove genocide, while that evidence is being actively erased? EYAL WEIZMAN : Yeah, absolutely. Genocide is a compounded crime of thousands, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of acts of violence, of murder, such as the story of Hind Rajab and the Hamadeh family, and the relation between them. Oftentimes Forensic Architecture spends months, sometimes a year, on a very careful analysis of a single incident. Here, I think that my team has watched tens of thousands of videos recorded by Palestinians, and reconstructed what is taking place. The help that Forensic Architecture is providing the South Africa legal team in the ICJ , the International Court of Justice in The Hague, is in building the bigger picture out of those multiplicity of crimes. So, take the Hind Rajab murder, for example. It is part of an attempt to empty, to depopulate, to ethnically cleanse Gaza City. The Hamadeh family — that is, the family where the uncles of Hind Rajab that actually drive the car — are ordered to leave Gaza City towards the south. At the same time that they are ordered to leave, all the hospitals are being attacked. The Al-Shifa Medical Complex, the largest in Palestine, is being destroyed. They are ordered to go south, to cross Wadi Gaza towards the south, the desert part of the Gaza Strip, while all the evacuation routes are being — Palestinians evacuating along them are being sniped at, shot by tanks, etc. So, you need to — with each one of those incidents, you need to see the larger context of what is happening at the same time. When you litigate a genocide — the Israeli side is trying to disaggregate the genocide into simply a multiplicity of actions that they claim may have been an attack that was aimed at Hamas fighters or another military maneuver at a particular point. And our attempt is to say what does it all add up to, how the bombing of the hospital relates to starvation that is created by the destruction of agriculture and the attack on aid coming in, the sniping and targeting by drones of Palestinians evacuating, how those different acts do not need to be considered each in itself, but have a compounded harm that is larger than the sum of its parts — i.e., if you are destroying agriculture, you deny a people ability to feed themselves. If at the same time you also hit an aid convoy, the effect of one amplifies the effect of another, and you generate famine. The famine is a means by which people are driven south towards those places that Israel provided a meager amount of food to starving Palestinians, drawing them towards the Egyptian border, where they’re entering into those death trap and sniped at. The entire genocide is an attempt to concentrate Palestinians next to the Egyptian border, where the majority are now located, and then with the next opportunity, when the border collapses or where people would receive permits to leave, or where people will be successfully, by Israel’s standards, be pushed out to empty Palestine out of Gaza — Palestinians. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Eyal Weizman, I’m wondering if you could put the — Israel’s massive destruction of Gaza into an even wider historical context. How does it compare, for example, to the Allied bombing of German cities in World War II or the U.S. firebombing of Tokyo or its carpet bombing of Vietnam and widespread use of Agent Orange and napalm against the Vietnamese? EYAL WEIZMAN : So, it includes all of those features. You had the destruction of — the use of defoliants has been practiced on Gaza since the 2010s, by which Israel has been using defoliants along the Gaza border in order to expose the areas for snipers. The mass bombing of cities has been in Gaza in the first weeks. Even in the first weeks, 25,000 tons of bombs has been dropped on Gaza, more than the entire aerial campaign on German cities. The result of the destruction is more total. I mean, you see entire neighborhoods completely destroyed and the rubble reshuffled. And so that we’re seeing the most intense use of arms, of explosives, of military equipment within a very, very small part. Remember, Germany is several thousand times the size of the Gaza Strip. And still, within that small area, you have a higher use of explosives. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And what is the most important thing you would like people to learn from this book? EYAL WEIZMAN : I’d like people to think about the use of the environment, both built and natural, as part of settler-colonial genocide. Historical settler-colonial genocide in the Americas, in southwest Africa, in Namibia, in many other places are about the transformation of the environment. The environment in the southwestern coast of Palestine is a very unique one. It’s the threshold of the desert. It’s the meeting point of agrarian areas and very dry areas. And that unique environmental conditions has been weaponized during the genocide. If you look at the direction of displacement of Palestinians, it’s always from the rain-rich north of Gaza and east of Gaza, where the alluvial soil is, towards the sand dunes on the more desert part of the strip. The kind of destruction and erasure of the environment has been one of the means to generate famine. So, you know, when we think about the Gaza Strip, in many people’s imagination, it is this overbuilt sea of concrete, etc. But the area is a very unique environmental — environment. And that particular environmental conditions have been weaponized to produce the genocide. The amount of toxin that has been released into the soil in Gaza is going to make that soil, that very fertile, rich agricultural soil, uncultivatable for generations. AMY GOODMAN : Eyal Weizman, I want to thank you so much for being with us, founder and director of Forensic Architecture, author of the new book Ungrounding: The Architecture of Genocide . That does it for our show. Tune in on election night — that’s Tuesday, November 3rd — for Democracy Now! ’s four-hour live election night special, starting at 8 p.m. Eastern election night through midnight Eastern time. Any radio or television station can take that four-hour midterm election special, or you can go to democracynow.org and beyond. Also, looking for a good movie to watch this weekend? The documentary about Democracy Now! , Steal This Story, Please! , is out on digital, all your streaming platforms, from Apple to Google Play, from Amazon Prime to YouTube and beyond. You can check it out, the documentary about the history of Democracy Now! and beyond. And I want to thank Denis Moynihan. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González. Thanks for joining us.

articles.author: Jamil Jonna
articles.content: In this election season, the MR Editors consider the history of U.S. interventions in foreign elections throughout the twentieth and twenty-first century and, in particular, the notable uptick in such meddling in the post-Cold War era. Throughout the capitalist world, Western “democracies”—which are democratic in form only and oligarchic in their content—continue to look away while the United States covertly and overtly engineers interference in elections around the globe on behalf of Trump-aligned, right-wing demagogues. articles.title: The Cultural Apparatus, Materialist Aesthetics, and the Critique of Eurocentrism
articles.author: Jamil Jonna
articles.content: John Bellamy Foster discusses the tradition of cultural analysis in Monthly Review with Jennifer Ponce de León and Gabriel Rockhill. “ MR ‘s approach…over its long history,” Foster explains, “has been a product of its deep commitment to historical materialism.” Drawing parallels between Bertolt Brecht’s observations during Hitler’s rise in Germany and an analysis of MAGA-style fascism under Trump today, it becomes clear that “control of the intellectual and cultural life of the nation is integral to the neofascist project.” However, there is also hope, as culture “constantly emerges from below in revolutionary new forms, which cannot be entirely repressed.” The post The Cultural Apparatus, Materialist Aesthetics, and the Critique of Eurocentrism appeared first on Monthly Review .

articles.title: Nietzsche’s French Legacy: Fascism and the Compatible Left
articles.author: Jamil Jonna
articles.content: MR is pleased to be able to share with readers Gabriel Rockhill’s Introduction to The Poverty of Left Nietzscheanism by Aymeric Monville (Iskra Books, 2026). Rockhill provides readers with a thorough account of the rehabilitation of Nietzsche within French Theory and its consequences within the non-communist left. Fascism, Rockhill argues, “can only be understood and contested through materialist analysis and anticapitalist praxis”—a fitting preamble to a book that acts as “an insightful indictment of the dominant capitalist ideologies while clearly articulating the political path forward.” The post Nietzsche’s French Legacy: Fascism and the Compatible Left appeared first on Monthly Review .

articles.title: Foreword to ‘The Exterminating Empire’
articles.author: Jamil Jonna
articles.content: In this stirring foreword to Chris Kaspar de Ploeg’s The Exterminating Empire (Monthly Review Press, 2026), Jason Hickel decries a world in which cruelty, genocide, and rapacious capitalism have become de rigueur, seemingly with no consequences for the Western elites perpetuating these atrocities in the Global South. “The narrative of ‘double standards,'” Hickel writes, “presupposes that they have at least some shred of morality. But they do not. For them there is but one standard: the law of capital.” The post Foreword to ‘The Exterminating Empire’ appeared first on Monthly Review .
